scenes.narration: We are asking whether the population mean recovery is the same for SPE methods A, B and C. If it is, their sample means can still differ because we only observe a finite number of preparations. Within each method, preparations vary around their own mean. That scatter gives us an estimate of error variance. Between the methods, sample means also fluctuate because of error. Under the classical model and equal population means, both mean squares estimate the same error variance on average. A large between-method mean square relative to the within-method mean square gives evidence against equal means.

scenes.narration: We want to know whether mean recovery changes when we switch preparation methods. The factor is what we vary: preparation method, with levels A, B and C. The response is what we measure: recovery in percent. For each method, six samples independently go through the full preparation, yielding six recovery values in this example. The groups can have different sizes. Aim for similar sizes so that each method is represented with comparable precision. The spread within each method therefore reflects both preparation and measurement variation. Ask what would happen if we prepared just one sample per method and injected each extract six times. Those technical replicates tell us about repeatability of the measurement on that extract. They cannot estimate how recovery varies across independent preparations with the same method.

scenes.narration: For each preparation, split the departure from the grand mean into a residual around its group mean and a departure of that group mean from the grand mean. The group-mean departure is constant within that group, so it can be taken outside the inner sum. The mixed term therefore vanishes after summation. This explains why the total sum of squares equals the between-group sum plus the within-group sum. scenes.narration: A sum of squares must be interpreted together with its degrees of freedom. Eighteen observations have seventeen independent departures around their fitted grand mean because those departures sum to zero. Three fitted group means supply two independent contrasts once the grand mean constraint is accounted for. Within each group, estimating one mean leaves five independent residual departures among six preparations. Across three groups, that gives fifteen residual degrees of freedom. The total seventeen therefore splits into two between-group and fifteen within-group degrees of freedom. This counting explains why the two sums of squares need different divisors before we compare them.

Their role is to place the two sources of variation on a comparable scale before forming a ratio.

On the next slide we will use that reference distribution to interpret the ratio. A zero error mean square leaves the ratio undefined under our teaching convention. The sums of squares quantify those contributions. The degrees of freedom count the independent deviations available for each source. The mean squares put the sources on a per-degree-of-freedom scale. Here the between-method mean square is twenty-one times the within-method mean square. The p-value tells us how rarely equal population means would produce an F at least this large under the model assumptions. This result gives evidence that at least one method mean differs. Next, inspect the residuals.

accessibility.label: Diagnose the residuals

blocks.text: Diagnose the residuals

blocks.alternativeText: A residual is observed recovery minus the fitted method mean. The table lists all 18 river-water preparations with observed recovery, fitted recovery, and residual. The normal Q-Q plot of these residuals compares the ordered decimal residuals with a normal reference line. In the schematic heavy-tail example, both ends depart strongly: the left tail falls far below the line and the right tail rises far above it. The descriptive KS distances to separate fitted normal distributions are 0.110 for the river-water residuals and 0.248 for the heavy-tail example. The Monte Carlo p-values are approximately 0.812 and 0.040, respectively, with model fitting repeated on each simulated sample.

blocks.text: In a normal Q-Q plot, look for systematic departures from the reference line.

blocks.alternativeText: NIST: One-factor ANOVA

scenes.narration: Take a preparation from Method A that measured 95.92 percent recovery against a fitted method mean of 94.00 percent. Its residual is plus 1.92 percentage points. The table shows all eighteen preparations, with one fitted value per method. The normal Q-Q plot compares the ordered decimal residuals with the reference line. The points broadly follow it. Compare this with the schematic heavy-tail example: the points in the middle stay near the line, but the left end falls far below it and the right end rises far above it. That pattern indicates more extreme residuals than a normal model would predict. The last view adds the Kolmogorov-Smirnov distance to a separately fitted normal curve. It is 0.110 for the river-water residuals and 0.248 for the schematic example. Each number is the largest vertical gap between two cumulative distributions. The simulated p-values are about 0.812 and 0.040, respectively. Each simulation refits the normal distribution. For the river-water data we also simulate three groups, round the recoveries as on the slide, and refit the group means before computing the residuals.

accessibility.label: How much of the spread is associated with method?

blocks.text: How much of the spread is associated with method?

blocks.alternativeText: Eighteen river-water recoveries by method. One overall prediction uses the grand mean of 95 percent. The method model uses group means of 94, 98, and 93 percent, leaving spread around each group mean.

blocks.text: Compare one overall recovery prediction with one prediction per method.

blocks.alternativeText: Lakens (2013): Eta squared

scenes.narration: Use the same eighteen river-water recoveries to ask how much method membership helps us describe the data. First fit one value to every preparation: the grand mean of 95 percent. The distances around that line capture all the observed spread. Now reveal one fitted mean for each method. For method B, the fit moves up to 98 percent. For method C, it moves down to 93 percent. The distances that remain are the within-method residuals. The next slide measures how much squared variation the method-specific fit removes.

accessibility.label: How much variation is explained?

blocks.text: How much variation is explained?

blocks.alternativeText: Using only the grand mean leaves 114 squared percentage points of residual spread. Using three method means leaves 30. The observed reduction of 84 divided by 114 is 73.7 percent.

entries.description: η² (eta squared) is the dimensionless share of observed variation attributed to the method factor. SS means sum of squared deviations; B is between methods and T is total.
84 is the between-method SS; 114 is total SS. Both are in squared percentage points.
The fraction bars divide. The equals signs show exact equality. ≈ means approximately equal after rounding to 0.73684.

blocks.text: Method explains 73.7% of the observed squared variation.

blocks.alternativeText: Lakens (2013): Eta squared

scenes.narration: Compare two predictions for each preparation. If we predict the grand mean for every preparation, the residual sum of squares is 114. If we instead predict the mean of the preparation's own method, the residual sum is 30. The second model reduces the observed squared error by 84. Divide this reduction by the original error, 114, to obtain eta squared: 0.737. So the method model accounts for 73.7 percent of the observed spread on the sum-of-squares scale. To judge whether that matters in practice, compare the actual recovery differences with the analytical requirements.

accessibility.label: Report the method effect

blocks.text: Report the method effect

blocks.alternativeText: One-way ANOVA for three methods with six independent preparations each. The overall test gives F 21 with 2 and 15 degrees of freedom, p about 0.00004484. The fitted method means account for 73.7 percent of observed squared variation. Compare individual effects with analytical tolerances.

blocks.text: Report the strength of the evidence and the size of the effect.

blocks.alternativeText: Lakens (2013): Eta squared

scenes.narration: Start with the design: three methods, each tested on six independent river-water preparations. The F statistic is 21 on 2 and 15 degrees of freedom, with p about 0.00004484. Under the model assumptions, that is evidence that at least one population mean differs. The fitted method means account for 73.7 percent of observed squared variation. This proportion is specific to these data and the fitted model. These results describe the river-water experiment. Next, use the same recoveries to ask whether a second grouping, by operator, would affect the interpretation.

accessibility.label: What if three operators processed the samples?

blocks.text: What if three operators processed the samples?

blocks.alternativeText: Hypothetical assignment of the 18 river-water samples. X processes three samples with method A and three with B. Y processes three with B and three with C. Z processes three with C and three with A. Each operator uses two methods, giving an incomplete block design.

blocks.text: Rotate the pairs so that every method is used by two operators.

blocks.alternativeText: Penn State: Incomplete block designs

scenes.narration: We can use an effect size to ask where a lab should look for variation. Imagine that three operators processed the same eighteen river-water samples. X used methods A and B, Y used B and C, and Z used C and A. Each operator processed three separately prepared samples per assigned method. That gives six observations per operator and six per method. For this teaching example, we attach hypothetical operator labels to the existing measurements. In a real study, plan and randomize the sample allocation within the allowed combinations before anyone sees the results.

accessibility.label: What changes when we regroup the recoveries?

blocks.text: What changes when we regroup the recoveries?

blocks.alternativeText: Both dot plots contain the same 18 river-water observations. By method the means are 94, 98, and 93 percent; p is approximately 0.00004484 and eta squared is 73.7 percent. By hypothetical operator the means are 95.93, 95.60, and 93.48 percent; p is 0.214 and eta squared is 18.6 percent. Color identifies the method in both plots.

blocks.text: The method mix can contribute to the apparent spread between operators.

blocks.alternativeText: Lakens (2013): Eta squared

scenes.narration: First group the eighteen recoveries by method. About 73.7 percent of observed squared variation lies between those method groups, and the overall p-value is about 0.00004484. Now group the same observations by the hypothetical operators. Their group means account for 18.6 percent of the observed squared variation, with p about 0.214. Notice that X and Y each used method B, while Z used A and C. The operator grouping therefore compares different mixtures of methods. The two eta-squared values describe different groupings of the same observations. To analyze two factors together, we now turn to a design that crosses each preparation method with each water matrix.

accessibility.label: Two-way ANOVA

blocks.text: Two-way ANOVA
How much variation can two factors explain?

scenes.narration: Add wastewater to the experiment so we can compare the same preparation methods in both water matrices. First fit the two factor effects additively, using the same steps as in the one-way ANOVA. Then check how the fit changes when we allow those effects to depend on each other.

accessibility.label: Add a second factor: water matrix

blocks.text: Add a second factor: water matrix

blocks.alternativeText: Three methods crossed with two water matrices, six independent preparations per combination. Stage one marks the existing river-water experiment and stage two adds wastewater, making 36 preparations.

blocks.text: Cross all three methods with both matrices.

blocks.alternativeText: NIST: Two-way ANOVA calculations

scenes.narration: Start with the same 18 river-water preparations. Each method was tested on six independent preparations. Now add wastewater as a second level of the matrix factor. Repeat the same three preparation methods with six independent wastewater preparations per method. Crossing the factors gives six method-by-matrix combinations and 36 observations. We can now ask two kinds of question: which overall averages change, and whether the method comparison itself changes between matrices. Each method and matrix combination needs its own independent preparations so that we can separate those effects from the residual spread.

accessibility.label: What do the 36 recoveries look like?

blocks.text: What do the 36 recoveries look like?

blocks.alternativeText: Thirty-six synthetic recovery measurements arranged by water matrix and preparation method. Each method and matrix combination has six measurements. Means in river water are 94, 98, and 93 percent. Means in wastewater are 92, 86, and 94 percent.

blocks.text: Each method–matrix combination has six independent recoveries.

blocks.alternativeText: NIST: Main effects and interaction

scenes.narration: Read the points as you did in the one-way example. Each dot is the measured recovery from one independent preparation. The left panel repeats the river-water groups. The right panel adds the same three methods in wastewater, on exactly the same recovery scale. Reveal the mean for each method in each matrix. Method B has a different mean in river water and in wastewater. As before, variation remains around each fitted mean. Next we will separate the variation associated with the two factors from what remains.

accessibility.label: Partition the sums of squares

blocks.text: Partition the sums of squares

blocks.alternativeText: The total sum of squares of 521 divides into method SS 14, matrix SS 169, and additive residual SS 338. The method and matrix contributions use weighted deviations of marginal means from the grand mean. The residual sums squared deviations of individual recoveries from their additive predictions.

blocks.spokenText: Partition total variation in the balanced design

entries.description: i indexes the three SPE methods, j the two water matrices, and k the six preparations within a combination. The sum runs over all combinations of these indices.
$y_{ijk}$ is an observed recovery in percent. $\hat{y}_{ij}$,add is its additive fitted value, using the grand mean plus the method and matrix shifts.
SSₜ is total SS, SSM is the method term, SSW is the water-matrix term, and SSE is the additive residual SS. Each is in squared percentage points.
Σ sums the indexed terms, plus adds, minus subtracts, parentheses group the residual, the superscript ² squares it, and = denotes equality.

blocks.text: The additive fit separates method, matrix and residual variation.

blocks.alternativeText: NIST: Two-way ANOVA calculations

scenes.narration: As in one-way ANOVA, calculate total variation as the sum of squared distances of all observations from the grand mean. Here the total is 521. The three method averages give a method sum of squares of 14, and the two matrix averages give a matrix sum of squares of 169. A method mean averages across both matrices, and a matrix mean averages across all methods. Each mean is weighted by the number of preparations behind it. The additive prediction combines the grand mean with the method and matrix shifts. Residual SS sums the squared distances from those predictions. It is 338. In this balanced design, the three contributions add to the total. Start the ANOVA table with these three rows.

accessibility.label: Build the additive ANOVA table

blocks.text: Build the additive ANOVA table

blocks.alternativeText: Additive ANOVA table. Method: SS 14, df 2, MS 7, F 0.663, p 0.5224, eta squared 2.69%. Matrix: SS 169, df 1, MS 169, F 16, p 0.000350, eta squared 32.44%. Residual: SS 338, df 32, MS 10.5625. Total: SS 521, df 35. Eta squared is the share of total SS associated with each factor.

blocks.text: Why is η² for method only 2.69%, and why is its F test no longer significant?

blocks.alternativeText: NIST: Two-way ANOVA calculations

scenes.narration: Start with the method and matrix sums of squares and the additive residual. The degrees of freedom count two method shifts and one matrix shift on top of the grand mean. With thirty-six observations, that leaves thirty-two for the residual. Divide each sum of squares by its degrees of freedom to obtain its mean square. The additive residual mean square is 10.5625. Use it as the denominator of both F ratios. Under additivity, these tests ask about the two common factor effects. Eta squared expresses each factor SS as a share of 521: 2.69% for method and 32.44% for water matrix. Why is the share for method so small, and why did its test change from significant to non-significant? Hold that question while we run the same comparison in a second study.

accessibility.label: A second example

blocks.text: A second example
To understand what happened in the two-way ANOVA, let's look at a different example.

scenes.narration: To understand what happened in the two-way ANOVA, let's look at a different example.

accessibility.label: Does the water treatment technique matter?

blocks.text: Does the water treatment technique matter?

blocks.alternativeText: In the illustrative NOM condition the measured removals are activated carbon 51, 55, 54, 56%; ultrafiltration 62, 66, 65, 67%; ion exchange 69, 73, 71, 75%.

blocks.text: How much of the spread is associated with the treatment technique?

blocks.alternativeText: NIST: One-factor ANOVA

scenes.narration: Start a separate teaching example with three water treatment techniques. In this first comparison, every run uses water with the same addition of natural organic matter, abbreviated NOM. Measure the percentage of a target contaminant removed in four independent runs for each technique. Each dot represents a separate run. The group means are 54, 65 and 72 percent. The graph suggests a difference, so the next step is to ask whether the separation is large compared with the scatter inside each technique.

accessibility.label: Build the one-way treatment ANOVA table

blocks.text: Build the one-way treatment ANOVA table

blocks.alternativeText: One-way ANOVA using the 12 NOM runs. The technique test is significant at the five percent level.

blocks.text: Under NOM addition, mean removal differs among the techniques.

blocks.alternativeText: NIST: ANOVA calculations

scenes.narration: Work through the table exactly as in the first example. First partition total variation into variation between techniques and variation within a technique. Then count degrees of freedom. Three techniques give two between-technique degrees of freedom, and twelve observations leave nine within-technique degrees of freedom. Divide each sum of squares by its degrees of freedom and compare the mean squares with the F ratio. The p-value is below 0.05. Under the NOM condition, at least one technique has a different mean removal.

accessibility.label: Add a second factor to the treatment study

blocks.text: Add a second factor to the treatment study

blocks.alternativeText: The crossed design has 36 independent runs, four per combination. Activated carbon, NOM addition: 51, 55, 54, 56%. Ultrafiltration, NOM addition: 62, 66, 65, 67%. Ion exchange, NOM addition: 69, 73, 71, 75%. Activated carbon, Phosphate addition: 58, 63, 61, 62%. Ultrafiltration, Phosphate addition: 68, 74, 71, 75%. Ion exchange, Phosphate addition: 76, 80, 77, 79%. Activated carbon, Ozone pretreatment: 68, 74, 70, 72%. Ultrafiltration, Ozone pretreatment: 76, 79, 78, 79%. Ion exchange, Ozone pretreatment: 88, 90, 86, 88%.

blocks.text: Three techniques × three water conditions gives nine combinations.

blocks.alternativeText: NIST: Two-way ANOVA calculations

scenes.narration: Now extend the study by crossing each treatment technique with three water conditions. One condition adds natural organic matter, one adds phosphate and one uses ozone pretreatment. These are three mutually exclusive levels of a single factor. A run has exactly one condition and exactly one technique. Each of the nine combinations has four independent runs. Keep the twelve NOM runs from the one-way comparison as the first column. The other two columns extend the comparison to the additional conditions.

accessibility.label: Build the additive treatment ANOVA table

blocks.text: Build the additive treatment ANOVA table

blocks.alternativeText: Additive ANOVA for water treatment. Both the technique and condition tests are significant at the five percent level.

blocks.text: Technique and water condition are both significant in the additive model.

blocks.alternativeText: NIST: Two-way ANOVA calculations

scenes.narration: Use all thirty-six runs. The additive table has one row for the technique and another row for the water condition. Both factors have three levels, so each gets two degrees of freedom. The remaining thirty-one degrees of freedom belong to the residual. Divide both factor mean squares by the same residual mean square. At the five percent level, both technique and water condition are significant in this model. The evidence for a technique effect remains after adding the second factor.

accessibility.label: Why does the conclusion change in only one study?

blocks.text: Why does the conclusion change in only one study?

blocks.alternativeText: Four ANOVA tables compare SPE recovery under river water alone and across both matrices, and removal under natural organic matter alone and across all conditions. A check mark indicates p below 0.05. A cross marks the SPE method in the additive model, with p = 0.522.

blocks.text: What changes in the SPE data that stays stable in the treatment data?

blocks.alternativeText: NIST: Two-way ANOVA calculations

scenes.narration: Read across the two rows. The first example asks about SPE method. It shows a clear method result in river water alone and no statistically significant common method effect when both matrices enter the additive model. The second example asks about treatment technique. It shows a clear technique result in the NOM runs and still shows a clear technique result when all water conditions enter the model. Both one-way tables use the reference condition shown in the earlier slides. What differs in the data?

accessibility.label: How do the gaps between group means change?

blocks.text: How do the gaps between group means change?

blocks.alternativeText: Stage one shows three technique profiles across ozone pretreatment, NOM addition and phosphate addition. The gaps vary while the rank order stays stable. Stage two shows crossing SPE profiles from wastewater to river water.

blocks.text: Do the gaps between lines stay about the same across conditions?

blocks.alternativeText: NIST: Interaction plots

scenes.narration: Start with the treatment data. Each line joins the means for a single technique, one point per condition. The horizontal axis lists categories. The connecting lines help compare the gaps, which vary a little while the techniques keep the same order. Then switch to the SPE data. Method B is four percentage points above A in river water and six percentage points below A in wastewater. The lines cross. The method difference changes with the matrix, so averaging over matrices can hide a strong difference within an individual matrix.

accessibility.label: When one factor changes the effect of another

blocks.text: When one factor changes the effect of another

blocks.alternativeText: Three schematic plots show widening gaps, nearly constant gaps, and narrowing gaps. Illustrative confidence intervals show uncertainty around each mean. The interaction test assesses whether the gaps change across conditions.

blocks.text: Does the gap change significantly across conditions?

blocks.alternativeText: NIST: Two-way ANOVA calculations

scenes.narration: Each plot compares two levels of factor A across two conditions of factor B. The brackets mark the differences between the means. On the left the gap widens, so the second condition strengthens the effect. On the right it narrows, so the second condition weakens the effect. In the middle the lines are nearly parallel. Sample means fluctuate, and the illustrative confidence intervals show uncertainty around each mean. Use the interaction test to assess whether the gap changes by more than we would expect from sampling variation.

accessibility.label: Where does the interaction sum of squares come from?

blocks.text: Where does the interaction sum of squares come from?

blocks.alternativeText: In the SPE study, the additive model assigns 14 to method, 169 to matrix and 338 to residuals. Adding the interaction splits 338 into 278 for method by matrix and 60 for the remaining residual. Total sum of squares stays at 521.

blocks.expression:
\begin{aligned}
\bar y_{ij\cdot}&=\frac{1}{r}\sum_{k=1}^{r}y_{ijk}\\
d_{ij}&=\underbrace{\bar y_{ij\cdot}}_{\text{mean for the combination}}-\underbrace{\Bigl(\overbrace{\bar y_{i\cdot\cdot}}^{\text{factor A mean}}+\overbrace{\bar y_{\cdot j\cdot}}^{\text{factor B mean}}-\overbrace{\bar y_{\cdot\cdot\cdot}}^{\text{grand mean}}\Bigr)}_{\text{reference from the factor means}}\\
SS_{AB}&=r\sum_{i=1}^{a}\sum_{j=1}^{b}d_{ij}^{2}=SS_{\mathrm{res,add}}-SS_W\\
SS_T&=SS_A+SS_B+SS_{AB}+SS_W
\\r&=\frac{N}{ab},\qquad \text{SPE: }r=\frac{36}{3\times 2}=6
\end{aligned}

entries.description:
- **$i$, $j$**: Levels of factors A and B that identify a combination.
- **$\bar y_{ij\cdot}$**: Observed mean for one combination. $y_{ijk}$ is recovery for preparation $k$ in that combination. A bar denotes a mean and a dot pools the corresponding index.
- **$\bar y_{i\cdot\cdot}$, $\bar y_{\cdot j\cdot}$**: Means across all runs at the indicated level of A or B.
- **$\bar y_{\cdot\cdot\cdot}$**: Overall mean of all runs. The means are expressed in percent.
- **$d_{ij}$**: Gap between the observed mean and its reference from the factor means, in percentage points.
- **$a$, $b$**: Numbers of levels of factors A and B, respectively.
- **$r$**: Number of independent runs per combination. Each combination has the same run count. In the SPE example, $r=6$.
- **$N$**: Total number of independent runs across all $ab$ combinations. Divide by $ab$ to get $r$.
- **$SS_T$, $SS_A$, $SS_B$**: Total sum of squares and sums of squares for the two factors.
- **$SS_{AB}$, $SS_W$**: Interaction sum of squares and remaining residual sum of squares. $SS_{\mathrm{res,add}}$ is the residual sum of squares in the additive model. All sums of squares are in squared percentage points.
- **$\sum$, $+,-,=,{}^2$**: Add across the indicated levels, add, subtract, equality and square. The multiplier $r$ weights each squared gap by its run count.

The formulas use a balanced design with the same number of runs for every combination.

blocks.text: The interaction explains part of the additive residual.

blocks.alternativeText: NIST: Two-way ANOVA calculations

scenes.narration: Start with the additive model for SPE recovery. Method and water matrix account for the first two parts. The rest is residual variation in that model. Adding method by matrix lets the model describe differences specific to combinations of method and water matrix. In this balanced design the main-effect sums of squares stay the same. The additive residual splits into 278 for the interaction and 60 that remain unexplained. The total stays 521. The formula tab shows how to calculate the split, and the next slide works it out from the measurements.

accessibility.label: Calculate the interaction sum of squares

blocks.text: Calculate the interaction sum of squares

blocks.alternativeText: Four steps use the SPE observations. Average six river-water recoveries for method B to get 98 percent. The additive reference is 94.17 percent and the deviation is about 3.83 percentage points. Use all six method and matrix combinations to get interaction SS 278. Subtract 278 from the additive residual 338 to leave 60.

blocks.text: The six weighted squared gaps account for 278 of the 338 additive residual.

blocks.alternativeText: NIST: Two-way ANOVA calculations

scenes.narration: Start with the six measured recoveries for method B in river water. Add them and divide by six to get ninety-eight percent. The additive reference combines the method and matrix means and subtracts the grand mean once. Subtract this reference from the observed mean to get a gap of about 3.83 percentage points. Repeat for all six combinations. Square each gap and multiply by six because there are six preparations in each combination. Add the six contributions using the unrounded values. The interaction sum of squares is 278, leaving 60 of the original 338 residual sum of squares.

accessibility.label: Build and test the interaction row in both studies

blocks.text: Build and test the interaction row in both studies

blocks.alternativeText: Both ANOVA tables show eta squared as the share of total sums of squares. SPE: method 2.69%, matrix 32.44%, interaction 53.36% (p = 5.4767e-12). Water treatment: technique 53.38%, condition 41.82%, interaction 0.79% (p = 0.28653). The SPE method is marked at 2.69% on a scale with rough benchmarks of 1% (small), 6% (medium), and 14% (large).

blocks.text: Test whether the interaction explains enough of the additive residual.

blocks.alternativeText: Lakens (2013): Eta squared

scenes.narration: Start with the additive residual in each study. Split it into variation assigned to the interaction and variation left as residual error. The interaction uses two degrees of freedom in the SPE example and four in the treatment example. The interaction accounts for 53.36 percent of total variation in the SPE example and 0.79 percent in the treatment example. For each study, divide the interaction mean square by the remaining residual mean square and read the p-value. At the five percent level we detect interaction for SPE recovery. The treatment example provides no significant evidence of interaction. That matches the contrast between crossing lines and profiles with smaller changes in their gaps.

accessibility.label: Post-hoc analysis

blocks.text: Post-hoc analysis
Which method means differ?

scenes.narration: An overall ANOVA can establish evidence that population means differ. We now follow up by comparing specific pairs of means.

accessibility.label: ANOVA found a difference. Where is it?

blocks.text: ANOVA found a difference. Where is it?

blocks.alternativeText: A significant ANOVA gives evidence that at least one population mean differs. Many post-hoc procedures exist. Tukey HSD compares every pair of group means.

blocks.text: ANOVA tests all means together. Post-hoc analysis identifies which pairs differ.

blocks.alternativeText: NIST Tukey HSD

scenes.narration: A significant ANOVA gives evidence that at least one population mean differs. Many post-hoc procedures exist. Tukey HSD compares every pair of group means. Start with the global question about the population means. If the overall test is significant, you still need a comparison that targets the differences you want to understand. In the next slides, we will consider three analytical methods and ask which pairs separate clearly. Tukey HSD is particularly useful when every pair is of interest and we want to interpret the comparisons together.

accessibility.label: Compare each gap with the HSD

blocks.text: Compare each gap with the HSD

blocks.alternativeText: Three analytical methods have five measurements each, with means 10, 12 and 17 mg/L. With an HSD of approximately 3.4 mg/L, C differs from A and B. The A–B result is inconclusive.

blocks.text: An absolute mean gap larger than the HSD is statistically significant.

blocks.alternativeText: NIST Tukey HSD

scenes.narration: Three analytical methods have five measurements each, with means 10, 12 and 17 mg/L. With an HSD of approximately 3.4 mg/L, C differs from A and B. The A–B result is inconclusive. First take the absolute difference so that the order of subtraction does not affect the decision. The gap of two is below the cutoff. The gaps of seven and five are above it, so method C differs from both other methods at this level. The smaller gap remains inconclusive. The next slide shows how the cutoff follows from the estimated error variance.

accessibility.label: Where does the Tukey cutoff come from?

blocks.text: Where does the Tukey cutoff come from?

blocks.alternativeText: The critical value is the 95th percentile of the studentized range distribution for three groups and 12 error degrees of freedom. With error mean square 4 and five observations per group, Tukey HSD is approximately 3.37 mg/L.

blocks.spokenText: Tukey HSD for equal group sizes

entries.description:
- **$HSD$**: The minimum absolute difference for significance, in the same units as the response.
- **$q_{crit}$**: The dimensionless upper critical value of the studentized range for the number of group means, the residual degrees of freedom, and the chosen familywise significance level.
- **$MS_E$**: The residual mean square from ANOVA, in squared response units.
- **$n$**: The common number of independent observations per group.
- **Operations**: The fraction divides the residual mean square by the group size. The square root restores the response units and multiplication by the critical value gives the cutoff.

blocks.text: More within-group scatter raises the cutoff. More observations lower it at fixed scatter.

blocks.alternativeText: Studentized range critical values
Studentized range distribution

scenes.narration: The critical value is the 95th percentile of the studentized range distribution for three groups and 12 error degrees of freedom. With error mean square 4 and five observations per group, Tukey HSD is approximately 3.37 mg/L. The distribution describes the range between the largest and smallest of the group means under the equal-means null, scaled by the estimated standard error. This is why its quantile depends on how many group means are in the family. Find three groups across the table and twelve residual degrees of freedom down the table to read 3.77 at the five percent level.

accessibility.label: SPE recovery: compare methods within each matrix

blocks.text: SPE recovery: compare methods within each matrix

blocks.alternativeText: One Tukey plot compares six intervals on a shared axis, with river water and wastewater paired for each method contrast. Each matrix is a separate 95% family. Both use the full model residual MSE of 2 and 30 error degrees of freedom. River water: HSD 2.01 percentage points. A versus B, adjusted p 8.978e-05. A versus C, adjusted p 0.4482. B versus C, adjusted p 2.902e-06. Wastewater: HSD 2.01 percentage points. A versus B, adjusted p 1.029e-07. A versus C, adjusted p 0.05175. B versus C, adjusted p 2.185e-10.

blocks.text: Method B has the highest mean in river water and the lowest mean in wastewater.

blocks.alternativeText: R Tukey HSD and simultaneous intervals

scenes.narration: One Tukey plot compares six intervals on a shared axis, with river water and wastewater paired for each method contrast. Each matrix is a separate 95% family. Both use the full model residual MSE of 2 and 30 error degrees of freedom. River water: HSD 2.01 percentage points. A versus B, adjusted p 8.978e-05. A versus C, adjusted p 0.4482. B versus C, adjusted p 2.902e-06. Wastewater: HSD 2.01 percentage points. A versus B, adjusted p 1.029e-07. A versus C, adjusted p 0.05175. B versus C, adjusted p 2.185e-10. The method ranking changes with the water matrix, so read the method comparisons within each matrix. The adjusted p-values protect the three contrasts within each matrix. In river water, method B has the highest mean. In wastewater it has the lowest. Check whether the intervals for the two contrasts involving method B cross zero, then compare that with the A versus C result.

sections.body:
Suppose three solid-phase extraction (SPE) methods are available for the same river-water sample. The analytical question is whether their **population mean recoveries** differ. A two-sample test addresses a specified pair. One-way ANOVA addresses the joint null hypothesis that all three population means are equal. Rejecting it gives evidence that at least one mean differs. Sample means can differ simply through sampling variation, so the separation must be judged against the scatter within each method.

The brackets in [[ref:ex:l7-script-two-to-three]] show how the scope changes from two samples to three groups. A significant pair and a significant overall ANOVA are different claims and depend on different test statistics. Adjustments such as Bonferroni control the error rate for a specified family of comparisons.

sections.title: From two means to several methods

sections.body:
**Preparation method** is the factor and **recovery (%)** is the response. Each of the three methods has six independent preparations. Several measurements of one preparation estimate measurement repeatability, while independent preparations capture the variation introduced by preparation itself. The three means are 94.00%, 98.00% and 93.00%, and the grand mean is 95.00%.

Subtract the grand mean from each observation to measure total variation. The resulting decomposition assigns 84 squared percentage points to differences between method means and 30 to scatter around those means. Their sum is 114. The between-method calculation weights each squared departure from the grand mean by the number of preparations in that method.

The F ratio in [[ref:ex:l7-script-formula-f]] compares the two mean squares in [[ref:ex:l7-script-level7-anova-read-table]]. Divide 84 by the two between-method degrees of freedom to get a mean square of 42. Divide 30 by the fifteen residual degrees of freedom to get 2. Their ratio is **F = 21**, with a right-tail p-value of about **0.00004484** under the equal-means null and the classical assumptions. The result points to a difference somewhere among the method means.

blocks.label: Between-group variation relative to within-group variation
blocks.spokenText: Divide the between-group mean square by the within-group mean square. A positive within-group mean square is required for this finite ratio.

entries.description:
- **F**: dimensionless omnibus test statistic.
- **$MS_B$**: group-size-weighted between-group sum of squares divided by (k−1), in percentage points squared.
- **$MS_W$**: residual within-group sum of squares divided by (N−k), in percentage points squared.
- **B/W**: subscripts meaning between groups/within groups.
- **k**: number of groups; k>1.
- **N**: total observations; N>k.
- **=**: equality.
- **fraction bar**: division of $MS_B$ by $MS_W$.

The fixed-effects model assumes independent Normal errors with a common positive variance. The omnibus test asks whether all population means are equal. $MS_W$ must be positive; F is undefined when this error mean square is zero.

sections.title: Design and compute the one-way ANOVA

sections.body:
A residual is observed recovery minus the fitted method mean. Classical ANOVA assumes independent errors with approximately normal distributions and common variance. Independence comes from the design. In a normal Q–Q plot, compare the ordered residuals with the reference line and look for systematic departures, including deviations at both tails. A test that estimates the normal parameters from the residuals needs calibration that accounts for fitting. The lecture illustrates this with refitting in a simulation.

The effect-size formula in [[ref:ex:l7-script-formula-eta]] relates the between-method sum of squares to the total. The one-way method effect accounts for **84 ÷ 114 = 73.7%** of the total sum of squares in this sample. This fraction is eta squared. It describes how much of the observed variation the grouping accounts for.

The regrouping exercise in [[ref:ex:l7-script-level7-anova-operator-grouping]] keeps the same observations and changes the labels to hypothetical operators. The operator groups use different mixes of preparation methods. Differences between these groups therefore combine operator labels with the method mix. Comparing their raw eta squared values does not isolate an operator effect.

sections.title: Check residuals and interpret the effect size

sections.body:
The SPE design crosses three preparation methods with two water matrices. Each combination has six independent preparations, for 36 in total. The additive model fits an overall difference between methods and an overall difference between matrices. It uses the same method differences in both matrices.

A second study crosses three treatment techniques with three water conditions: natural organic matter addition, phosphate addition and ozone pretreatment. Each combination contains four independent runs. The response is contaminant removal (%).

Read across [[ref:ex:l7-script-level7-anova-four-tables]] to see what changes as a second factor enters the analysis. The river-water method comparison is clear in the one-way analysis, while the additive comparison across both matrices gives p = 0.522. In the treatment study, the technique effect remains significant after adding the water condition. To understand these patterns, examine the mean profiles and test interaction.

sections.title: Add a second factor

sections.body:
An interaction means that the difference between levels of one factor changes across levels of another. For the SPE data, method B exceeds method A by 4.00 percentage points in river water and falls below it by 6.00 points in wastewater. The direction reverses. The treatment profiles are closer to parallel, so the difference between techniques is more stable across conditions. In the balanced design, [[ref:ex:l7-script-formula-interaction]] shows how to turn those departures from the additive pattern into a sum of squares.

For each method and matrix combination, the additive reference is its method mean plus its matrix mean minus the grand mean. For method B in river water these three values are 92.00%, 95.00% and 92.83%. The resulting reference is 94.17% and the observed mean is 98.00%. The interaction gap is about +3.83 percentage points. Square the unrounded gap and multiply by the six independent preparations to get this combination’s contribution, about 88.17 squared percentage points. Repeat for all six combinations and add the contributions.

In [[ref:ex:l7-script-level7-anova-interaction-test]], adding the interaction assigns 278 of the additive residual sum of squares of 338 to the interaction and leaves 60. The overall sum of squares stays at 521. In this balanced design the method sum of squares also stays fixed. Its p-value drops to 0.043 as the residual mean square decreases, while its eta squared remains 2.69%. The interaction accounts for 53.36% of the total variation. For treatment, the interaction accounts for 0.79% and gives p = 0.287. The 1%, 6% and 14% marks are Cohen’s rough benchmarks as discussed by Lakens (2013). Practical importance depends on which recovery differences matter for the application.

\begin{aligned}
\bar y_{ij\cdot}&=\frac{1}{r}\sum_{k=1}^{r}y_{ijk}\\
d_{ij}&=\underbrace{\bar y_{ij\cdot}}_{\text{mean for the combination}}-\underbrace{\Bigl(\overbrace{\bar y_{i\cdot\cdot}}^{\text{factor A mean}}+\overbrace{\bar y_{\cdot j\cdot}}^{\text{factor B mean}}-\overbrace{\bar y_{\cdot\cdot\cdot}}^{\text{grand mean}}\Bigr)}_{\text{reference from the factor means}}\\
SS_{AB}&=r\sum_{i=1}^{a}\sum_{j=1}^{b}d_{ij}^{2}=SS_{\mathrm{res,add}}-SS_W\\
SS_T&=SS_A+SS_B+SS_{AB}+SS_W
\\r&=\frac{N}{ab},\qquad \text{SPE: }r=\frac{36}{3\times 2}=6
\end{aligned}

entries.description:
- **$i$, $j$**: Levels of factors A and B that identify a combination.
- **$\bar y_{ij\cdot}$**: Observed mean for one combination. $y_{ijk}$ is recovery for preparation $k$ in that combination. A bar denotes a mean and a dot pools the corresponding index.
- **$\bar y_{i\cdot\cdot}$, $\bar y_{\cdot j\cdot}$**: Means across all runs at the indicated level of A or B.
- **$\bar y_{\cdot\cdot\cdot}$**: Overall mean of all runs. The means are expressed in percent.
- **$d_{ij}$**: Gap between the observed mean and its reference from the factor means, in percentage points.
- **$a$, $b$**: Numbers of levels of factors A and B, respectively.
- **$r$**: Number of independent runs per combination. Each combination has the same run count. In the SPE example, $r=6$.
- **$N$**: Total number of independent runs across all $ab$ combinations. Divide by $ab$ to get $r$.
- **$SS_T$, $SS_A$, $SS_B$**: Total sum of squares and sums of squares for the two factors.
- **$SS_{AB}$, $SS_W$**: Interaction sum of squares and remaining residual sum of squares. $SS_{\mathrm{res,add}}$ is the residual sum of squares in the additive model. All sums of squares are in squared percentage points.
- **$\sum$, $+,-,=,{}^2$**: Add across the indicated levels, add, subtract, equality and square. The multiplier $r$ weights each squared gap by its run count.

The formulas use a balanced design with the same number of runs for every combination.

sections.title: Test whether the factor effects depend on each other

sections.body:
Tukey HSD compares all pairs of group means within a specified family. For equally sized groups, use [[ref:ex:l7-script-formula-hsd]]. Multiply the critical studentized range value by the square root of the ANOVA residual mean square divided by the number of observations per group. The studentized range is the spread from the smallest to the largest group mean under the equal-means null, scaled by the estimated standard error of one mean. The cutoff depends on the family’s number of groups, the residual degrees of freedom and the chosen error rate.

Take three methods with means of 10, 12 and 17 mg/L, five observations each and a residual mean square of 4 squared mg/L. At the 5% level, the reference table gives 3.77 for three groups and 12 residual degrees of freedom. The HSD is 3.37 mg/L. The gaps of 7 and 5 mg/L exceed this threshold. The gap of 2 mg/L leaves the A–B comparison inconclusive.

In [[ref:ex:l7-script-level7-anova-post-hoc-spe]], each water matrix has its own Tukey family of three method comparisons, using the residual mean square of the full SPE model. The matrix gives adjusted p-values and the plot shows signed differences with simultaneous 95% intervals within each matrix. Intervals excluding zero identify significant comparisons. Method B differs from both A and C in each matrix, with the direction reversed. The A–C intervals include zero in both matrices.

entries.description:
- **$HSD$**: The minimum absolute difference for significance, in the same units as the response.
- **$q_{crit}$**: The dimensionless upper critical value of the studentized range for the number of group means, the residual degrees of freedom, and the chosen familywise significance level.
- **$MS_E$**: The residual mean square from ANOVA, in squared response units.
- **$n$**: The common number of independent observations per group.
- **Operations**: The fraction divides the residual mean square by the group size. The square root restores the response units and multiplication by the critical value gives the cutoff.
